intro: Artur Schnabel plays the Appassionata’s quiet centre: a D♭-major tune whose plain chords blossom into ever quicker notes. At the end, one diminished seventh opens the door to the finale.

sections.label: Theme · Low D♭-major chords
sections.mNote: Two eight-bar halves, each played twice

sections.label: Var 1 · Chords before the bass
sections.mNote: Upper chords strike first; the bass answers off the beat

sections.label: Var 2 · Flowing semiquavers
sections.mNote: The right hand spreads each chord into a flowing line

sections.label: Var 3 · Demisemiquavers change hands
sections.mNote: The tune sings above, then below, the quickest notes

sections.label: Theme · The plain chords return
sections.mNote: The theme returns without its repeats

sections.label: Link · Two diminished sevenths
sections.mNote: Rolled chords under fermatas lead straight into the finale

cues.title: A tune close to earth
cues.text: Both hands begin low on the keyboard. D♭-major chords move in a measured two-beat tread, with small dotted figures at the ends of phrases. Each eight-bar half comes round twice.
cues.evidence: Schott Einzelausgabe, Andante con moto, bars 1–16, as transcribed by Andreas Scherer for Mutopia: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=288
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: The hands part company
cues.text: The first variation pulls the hands apart. The upper chord sounds on the beat; the bass answers afterwards and hangs across the next beat. The same tune has acquired a gentle, persistent tug.
cues.evidence: Schott Einzelausgabe, bars 17–35: upper chords alternate with the syncopated bass. Mutopia’s transcription preserves the separate hands and tied bass notes.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Marie Bigot’s wet manuscript
cues.text: In Paul Bigot’s account, Beethoven arrives at their Vienna home carrying the sonata’s rain-soaked manuscript. Marie Bigot sits down and plays through its erasures and corrections. Beethoven promises her the manuscript and brings it back after the engraver has finished with it.
cues.evidence: Paul Bigot’s recollection, reproduced by Beethoven-Haus under the composition history of Op. 57. The surviving autograph belonged to Marie Bigot and bears water stains: https://www.beethoven.de/en/work/view/5292968940404736

cues.title: Chords become a stream
cues.text: The right hand unfolds the tune into semiquavers. Underneath, the left hand keeps the slower steps of the D♭-major theme. The pianist now plays four notes in the space once occupied by one.
cues.evidence: Schott Einzelausgabe, bars 36–53: semiquaver arpeggios in the right hand above the theme’s bass.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Eight notes to the beat
cues.text: Demisemiquavers pour through the left hand while the tune hangs above them in longer notes. Later the hands exchange jobs. The quick notes climb high on the keyboard, then tumble back towards the opening chords.
cues.evidence: Schott Einzelausgabe, bars 54–85: demisemiquavers first below the melody, then above it; the variation ends in a descending run.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: The theme comes home
cues.text: The plain chords return in D♭ major. Beethoven leaves out the repeats and lets phrases answer one another across the keyboard: low chords, then a reply an octave higher.
cues.evidence: Schott Einzelausgabe, bars 86–100: unrepeated theme with octave displacements.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: The wrong last chord
cues.text: The expected D♭-major chord never comes. E–G–B♭–D♭ sounds instead: a diminished seventh, rolled and held under a fermata. Beethoven repeats it an octave higher. The finale begins on that same chord.
cues.evidence: Schott Einzelausgabe, bars 101–102, gives the two rolled diminished sevenths. The opening of movement III repeats the harmony; the first edition marks attacca between the movements.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

transitions.title: The hands strike separately
transitions.how: The theme closes on D♭. The first variation begins with the same upper chords, but the left hand enters a quaver after the right and ties its notes across the beat. Both hands keep the tune’s harmonic steps while their attacks pull apart.
transitions.evidence: Schott Einzelausgabe, bars 15–20; Andreas Scherer’s Mutopia transcription: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=288

transitions.title: The right hand begins to flow
transitions.how: The first variation reaches D♭ major and leaves a brief rest. The right hand begins again high on the keyboard, breaking the chords into semiquavers. The left hand returns to the theme’s slower bass, beginning on D♭.
transitions.evidence: Schott Einzelausgabe, bars 35–38: close of the first variation and opening arpeggios of the second.

transitions.title: The quick notes change hands
transitions.how: The second variation closes in D♭ major. A demisemiquaver pickup starts in the left hand, and the right hand stretches the melody into longer, syncopated notes. The smallest written note-value has halved again; the theme’s bass and cadences remain in place.
transitions.evidence: Schott Einzelausgabe, bars 53–56: left-hand demisemiquaver pickup and syncopated right-hand melody.

transitions.title: The run lands on the theme
transitions.how: The demisemiquavers descend through the keyboard. At the bottom, the run meets the D♭ bass of the returning theme. Plain right-hand chords restore the opening’s measured tread, and the melody begins its last statement without repeats.
transitions.evidence: Schott Einzelausgabe, bars 83–88: descending run and return of the theme.

transitions.title: D♭ becomes a dissonance
transitions.how: The last cadence turns away from D♭ major into E–G–B♭–D♭, with B♭ at the bottom. The pianist rolls the chord and holds it under a fermata, then repeats it an octave higher. The first edition’s attacca sends this unresolved diminished seventh directly into the finale.
transitions.evidence: Schott Einzelausgabe, bars 100–102. First edition, Bureau des Arts et d’Industrie, plate 521, pp. 16–17, marks attacca: https://www.beethoven.de/en/media/view/6661552451092480?page=0

fields.label: Performers
fields.note: Archive description, embedded artist tag and discography agree. Bloesch identifies a Bechstein piano in Studio No. 3 for the session; no instrument serial number is established.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: The original solo-piano movement is identified, but Schnabel’s performing edition and editorial alterations are not documented. The listening commentary uses the viewable original edition, plate 521; that does not establish the score used in 1933. The musical attacca into movement III is distinguished from the spacing of the separately hosted MP3 files.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The Archive’s sonata-specific description gives 11.IV.1933, corroborated by Bloesch and the reissue documentation. The compilation-level date 1932 is not adopted for this movement. Neither the embedded 2001 tag nor the 2020 repository upload establishes a session or transfer date.

fields.label: Place
fields.value: Abbey Road Studios, Studio No. 3, London, England
fields.note: The chronological session list identifies Studio No. 3 and a Bechstein; the work entry identifies Abbey Road Studios, London.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: The historical original issue was on His Master’s Voice, but the carrier or later reissue actually transferred for this MP3 is not named. The original label is not substituted for that missing link.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The original complete-sonata issue was HMV DB 2215–2217 in Beethoven Sonata Society Volume 5, within set DB 2211–2217. The selected digital file does not identify the pressing or reissue from which it was made; its source-carrier catalogue number remains unknown.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.note: Bloesch assigns the Andante to historical sides 2B 6607 and 2B 6608; the issued takes are listed as 1, matching catalogue entries 2B 6607I and 2B 6608I. Bloesch also records a change in the selection history of 2B 6608. The MP3’s actual take selection and side-join location have not independently been established.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: No engineer is credited for the selected MP3. The uploader recordplayer78 is not identified as the transfer engineer or rights owner. Andrew Rose’s credit belongs to the separately documented Pristine reissue, not automatically to this file. No upstream link between the two transfers is established.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: Archive added/public date: 27 March 2020. Embedded date tag: 2001, with no documented release or transfer referent. Neither is used as the analogue-transfer date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: The embedded encoder tag states ‘Audiograbber 1.83.01, LAME dll 3.99, 256 Kbit/s, Joint Stereo, Normal quality’.
fields.note: The downloaded selected stream has MP3 audio at 44,100 Hz, two channels and 256,000 bit/s, with an attached JPEG image. Two-channel encoding is not evidence of an original stereo recording. Analogue equipment, equalisation, restoration, noise reduction, speed/pitch correction and edit history are unknown. Archive’s generic ‘VBR MP3’ inventory label is kept separate from the inspected stream and encoder tag.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: The underlying Beethoven composition is public domain under the ordinary EU life-plus-70 term.
fields.note: Beethoven died in 1827. The historical score is distinct from any unidentified modern performing edition. The composition’s term does not establish the rights in Schnabel’s recording.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3 — territorial EU public domain: original sound recording first published in 1934.
fields.note: The Public Domain Project release-set catalogue explicitly dates first release of HMV DB 2211–2217 to 1934. Bloesch identifies the Appassionata issue as DB 2215–2217, matrices 2B 6605–6610, establishing publication separately from the 11 April 1933 recording date. Under the programme’s territorial EU rule, the earlier 50-year term expired before the 2013 extension. US status is not established; no worldwide clearance is claimed. Archive’s Public Domain Mark is not an ownership release, and the Public Domain Project’s worldwide/US expiry table is not relied upon. No CC licence or independently established additional rights in an unidentified modern transfer are asserted.

dossier.credit: Ludwig van Beethoven, Piano Sonata No. 23, Op. 57, II. Andante con moto — Artur Schnabel, piano; recorded 11 April 1933, Abbey Road Studio No. 3, London. Originally issued by HMV in Beethoven Sonata Society Volume 5; selected MP3 through Internet Archive item beethovenschnabel6. Transferred carrier and engineer unknown. Territorial EU recording basis; US status not established.

composer.epithet: He could make a symphony out of four notes, and spent his last years finding things four string players had never said.
facts: Neefe in Bonn; Haydn, Albrechtsberger and Salieri in Vienna
Bonn until 1792; Vienna and its surrounding villages for the rest of his life
Nine symphonies · five numbered piano concertos · 32 numbered piano sonatas · 16 string quartets · Fidelio
Described his hearing loss in 1801; used conversation books from 1818

quote.text: I live only in my notes.
quote.source: Beethoven to Franz Gerhard Wegeler, Vienna, 29 June 1801; our translation

composer.background:
In March 1778 Johann van Beethoven advertised a concert in Cologne by his six-year-old son. Ludwig was seven. His father, a singer in the electoral chapel at Bonn, hoped to launch another child prodigy; his grandfather, also Ludwig, had risen from singer to Kapellmeister in the same establishment. The boy was baptised on 17 December 1770, probably the day after his birth. Music was the family trade. By his teens he was playing the organ for services and the viola in the court orchestra, learning operas from the middle of the string section.

Christian Gottlob Neefe put Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier before him and helped him into paid employment. The Breuning household supplied books, friendship and a refuge from Johann’s drinking. After his mother died in 1787, Beethoven increasingly supported his younger brothers. In November 1792 the elector sent him to Vienna to study with Haydn. He was supposed to come back. French troops occupied Bonn in 1794, and the court that paid him disappeared.
